title: India's Biodiversity Hotspots

endcard.line: Pictures: Shrinivas Ayyangar (CC BY 4.0); Anshulsawant (public domain); Tej Bhat (CC BY 4.0); rohitnaniwadekar (CC BY 4.0)

segments.say: These forested hills hold plants found nowhere else on Earth. They are part of one of India's four biodiversity hotspots.

anim.title: Two tests for a hotspot
items: At least 1,500 plant species found only there
At least 70% of original vegetation lost

segments.say: To count as a hotspot, a region must pass two tests. It must have at least fifteen hundred plant species found nowhere else, and it must have lost at least seventy per cent of its original vegetation.
So a hotspot is both very rich and badly threatened. The ecologist Norman Myers proposed the idea in nineteen eighty-eight. Today thirty-six are recognised.
India has four. The first is the Himalaya.
The second is Indo-Burma, which takes in the north-east. The third is the Western Ghats, shared with Sri Lanka. The fourth is Sundaland.
Sundaland reaches India only at the Nicobar Islands, far out in the Bay of Bengal's south-east.
India covers about two point four per cent of the world's land, yet holds seven to eight per cent of its known species.
For Prelims, remember the two tests and the four names. And note the count has grown, from thirty-four to thirty-six.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Biodiversity hotspot' (read): Norman Myers wrote about the concept in 1988 and 1990, revised in 2000; a hotspot must have at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and must have lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation

PIB, MoEFCC release on the IUCN World Conservation Congress (PRID 2176948): India is among 17 megadiverse countries and home to four of the 36 global hotspots: the Himalayas, the Western Ghats, Indo-Burma and Sundaland

PIB note 'India's Wildlife Conservation Milestones' (NoteId 153834): India covers 2.4% of the Earth's land and is home to 7–8% of known species; four of the world's 34 hotspots, naming the Himalayas, Western Ghats, the Northeast and the Nicobar Islands

quiz.q: Which is one of the two criteria for a biodiversity hotspot?
options: A national park larger than 1,000 km²
quiz.why: At least 1,500 endemic vascular plants and at least 70% of primary vegetation lost.

quiz.q: Which hotspot reaches India only through the Nicobar Islands?
quiz.why: PIB names the Nicobar Islands for Sundaland.

quiz.q: How many global biodiversity hotspots are recognised now, per the 2025 PIB release?
quiz.why: Four of the 36 global hotspots are in India; 34 is an older count.

reviewNote: No map is used, as the brief asks. Facts are from two PIB pages (which give 34 and 36; the script uses 36 and explains the change) and the Wikipedia article for the criteria and Myers. Check the criteria wording against Conservation International or CEPF before approval (the CEPF page didn't return text here). 'Bay of Bengal's south-east' is a plain description; check it reads right, or cut to 'far out to sea'. Moving facts: the global hotspot count.
